message.content: Reality is a small, prickly thing that refuses to dissolve into beauty without a body. In the country of All Surfaces, the sky was a smear of cobalt and rust, the hills were torn triangles, and the rivers were sentences without grammar. No one—because no one had anyone to ask—knew whether the world was painted, dreamed, or merely arranged. In the center of a meadow of floating brushstrokes walked a hedgehog with round, brass-rimmed glasses, his tiny paws leaving the only true footprints for miles. Abstractness can imitate life, but it cannot tremble before the wind. When a spiral of violet mist leaned toward him, the hedgehog flinched, and the mist, having never met flinching, stuttered into a new shape. A red polygon hummed a chord that tasted like Tuesday. A grid of silver lines bowed to him, then unfolded into a door with no wall. He stepped through because, being real, he understood that doors are promises, even in a place where nothing had to be kept. The glasses are not there to make the world neat, but to prove that it can be looked at. He pushed the lenses up his snout and saw what the colors wanted to become: a forest of impossible angles, a mountain made of overlapping circles, a sea of pale rectangles that rippled when he breathed. The world admired itself, the way a painting admires its own frame. The hedgehog admired it too, but with a different kind of love—the love of a creature who can be hurt, who can blink, and who knows that clarity is a small rebellion against infinity. Only the real can be lonely in a world full of figures. A long, black line curled around him like a cat made of shadow and asked, in a voice like dry paper, “Do you belong to the pattern?” “No,” he said. “I belong to my own shadow.” The line laughed, or perhaps the laughter was a sudden grid of yellow stars. “Then you are the error,” it said, “or the only proof.” He did not know which frightened him more, so he kept walking, because walking is what real things do when they do not yet know the answer. Absence of consequence does not make a world kind; it makes it strange. He crossed a desert of torn canvases, where flowers opened and closed in wrong sequences and a storm of blue circles forgot how to fall. A broken archway spoke to him in fragments: “Stay. Become a symbol. Be the point that gives the whole its center.” But the hedgehog remembered that symbols can be mistaken for things, and things are responsible for their own small lives. He drank from a puddle that was more idea than water, felt his thirst remain thirst, and knew he was still himself. The world may be abstract art, but a real creature can teach it what it means to matter. At last he reached a clearing of white nothing, where all the colors gathered like silent animals around a fire. They pressed their edges toward him, trying to become soft, trying to become warm, trying to become the creature that could say “I am here” without merely being placed. The hedgehog sat, adjusted his glasses, and blinked. In that blink, the abstract world received a single, unmistakable fact: a small heart, beating in the center of beauty, and the sudden, startling sense that it had been waiting to be seen.
